name: Greedy policy from action values
intuition: With action values, improvement needs no model: just pick the action with the largest value.
pitfalls: With state values instead, the same step would need p(s′, r|s, a) for a one-step look-ahead.

verification.note: Printed p. 121 (PDF p. 135), checked on the page image.

name: ε-greedy improvement over an ε-soft policy
tex: q_\pi(s, \pi'(s)) = \sum_a \pi'(a|s) q_\pi(s, a) = \frac{\epsilon}{|\mathcal{A}(s)|}\sum_a q_\pi(s, a) + (1 - \epsilon)\max_a q_\pi(s, a)
intuition: The ε-greedy policy spreads ε uniformly and puts the rest on the best action; that is at least the value of any ε-soft policy's own average, so the policy improvement theorem applies.
assumptions: π is ε-soft: π(a|s) ≥ ε/|A(s)| for every action.

derivation.why: The weights (π(a|s) − ε/|A(s)|)/(1 − ε) are nonnegative (π is ε-soft) and sum to 1, so their average is at most the maximum.

derivation.tex: q_\pi(s, \pi'(s)) \ge \frac{\epsilon}{|\mathcal{A}(s)|}\sum_a q_\pi(s, a) - \frac{\epsilon}{|\mathcal{A}(s)|}\sum_a q_\pi(s, a) + \sum_a \pi(a|s) q_\pi(s, a) = v_\pi(s)
derivation.why: Add the uniform part back; it cancels, leaving π's own average of its action values.

pitfalls: The improvement only reaches the best ε-soft policy, not π_*.

verification.note: Printed p. 125 (PDF p. 139), checked on the page image. Checked numerically by ch05.epsilon-greedy-improvement.

name: Importance-sampling ratio
intuition: How much more (or less) likely the observed trajectory is under the target policy than under the behavior policy. The unknown transition probabilities cancel.
example: In Example 5.4 the behavior picks hit or stick with probability 1/2 and the target is deterministic, so a game that follows the target for three decisions has $\rho = 2^3 = 8$; any game where the behavior deviates has $\rho = 0$.
pitfalls: If the target is deterministic, ρ is 0 as soon as the behavior takes an action the target would not.

verification.note: Printed p. 128 (PDF p. 142), checked on the page image. The cancellation is checked by ch05.is-ratio-model-free.

name: Ordinary importance sampling

symbols.meaning: the time steps at which s is visited (first visits only, for a first-visit method)

intuition: Scale each return by its ratio and take a plain average.
assumptions: Time steps are numbered across episodes, so each visit has its own t.
pitfalls: Unbiased, but the variance can be infinite (Example 5.5).

verification.note: Printed p. 128 (PDF p. 142), checked on the page image. Unbiasedness checked by ch05.ordinary-is-unbiased.

name: Weighted importance sampling

symbols.meaning: the ratio for the return after t

intuition: Use the ratios as weights in a weighted average. After one return the estimate is just that return.
assumptions: Defined as 0 when the denominator is 0.
pitfalls: Biased (after one return its expectation is v_µ(s)), but the bias vanishes as returns accumulate, and with bounded returns its variance goes to zero.

verification.note: Printed p. 129 (PDF p. 143), checked on the page image.

name: Weighted average of returns

symbols.meaning: the weight of the k-th return, e.g. its importance-sampling ratio

intuition: The estimate after n − 1 returns, each with its own weight.
pitfalls: With every W_k = 1 this is the sample average of Chapter 2.

verification.note: Printed p. 133 (PDF p. 147), checked on the page image.

name: Incremental weighted-average update
tex: V_{n+1} = V_n + \frac{W_n}{C_n}\big[G_n - V_n\big], \quad n \ge 1, \qquad C_{n+1} = C_n + W_{n+1}, \; C_0 = 0

symbols.meaning: the sum of the first n weights

intuition: Move the estimate toward the new return by its share of the total weight so far.
pitfalls: A return with weight 0 leaves V unchanged.

verification.note: Printed p. 133 (PDF p. 147), checked on the page image. Checked against the batch average by ch05.incremental-weighted.

name: A return as a sum of flat partial returns
tex: \bar G_t^h = R_{t+1} + \cdots + R_h, \qquad G_t = \gamma^{T-t-1}\bar G_t^T + (1 - \gamma)\sum_{h=t+1}^{T-1} \gamma^{h-t-1} \bar G_t^h

symbols.meaning: the flat (undiscounted) partial return up to horizon h

intuition: Discounting is read as a chance of stopping: the return stops after one step with weight 1 − γ, after two with (1 − γ)γ, and so on.
assumptions: 0 ≤ γ < 1, an episode ending at T.
pitfalls: The weights sum to 1: (1 − γ)(1 + γ + … + γ^{T−t−2}) + γ^{T−t−1} = 1.

verification.note: Printed unnumbered on p. 137 (PDF p. 151), checked on the page image. The identity is checked by ch05.flat-partial-returns.

name: Ordinary importance sampling on truncated returns

symbols.meaning: the ratio of the steps up to horizon h only

intuition: Each flat partial return is scaled only by the ratios of the actions that produced it.
assumptions: γ < 1; with γ = 1 it reduces to (5.4).
pitfalls: The truncated ratios matter most when γ is small and episodes long.

verification.note: Printed p. 137 (PDF p. 151), checked on the page image.

name: Weighted importance sampling on truncated returns
intuition: The weighted counterpart: the same numerator, divided by the same combination of truncated ratios.
pitfalls: Exercise 5.10 asks for the action-value version inside off-policy control.

verification.note: Printed p. 137 (PDF p. 151), checked on the page image.
